title: Navigation for a restaurant group
metaTitle: Navigation for a restaurant group site
excerpt: Menu labels should be the jobs a guest has tonight: pick a restaurant, read the menu, book a table. One path has to reach that table without a riddle.
alt: A white geometric building with a glass wing and a cantilevered upper volume, a structure whose entrance only works if you can tell which volume you are meant to enter.
caption: A building with more than one volume. The menu should still name the door. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What belongs in the header?
faqs.answer: Use the jobs a guest already has words for: the restaurants by name, menus, book a table, and private dining if it is real. Story, journal, and press can wait off that list until a guest can find dinner without opening a second panel. If a label needs a translation, it is not ready for the header.

faqs.question: How should several restaurants appear?
faqs.answer: As names a local would say, not as a single item called Concepts. If you have three rooms, three text links are clearer than a map of pins. Each link should land on that room with its hours, menu, and booking already aimed there.

faqs.question: Where does Book live?
faqs.answer: In the header, and again on each restaurant, with the venue already chosen. One generic Book that forgets which room is a trap. On a phone, the action should be reachable without hunting through a film.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
Good restaurant group website navigation is a map of jobs, not a list of brand departments. A guest deciding where to go tonight already has the words. The restaurants, by the names people say. Menus. A way to book a table. The labels should match those words. One path should reach the menu or the table without a riddle.

A poetic menu reassures the workshop that the group has a voice. It slows the guest who is texting a friend from the sidewalk. They should not have to decode you before they can eat.

## Jobs a guest has tonight

List the reasons the site gets opened. Which room. What is on the menu. Whether a table is bookable. Sometimes, a private room. Those are the items. "Experience," "World," "Journal," and "Explore" are departments the brand invented.

A practical primary list:

- Restaurants, or the actual names if you only have a few
- Menus
- Book a table
- Private dining, if you sell it

Four is plenty. Add a story link only when that page helps a guest choose, and keep it off the first position. The first position is dinner.

[The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) groups requirements under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. Navigation has to be understandable: a control should say where it goes, a keyboard user should reach it, and the items should stay in familiar places. Clever labels fail that test first. A guest using a screen reader should hear "Holt Street," not "canvas one."

[Google's guidance on title links](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/title-link) asks for descriptive, concise titles. Menu items deserve the same standard. "Menus" is concise and true. "Paper" is a guessing game. If the page heading and the menu item disagree, fix the menu. The guest remembers what they tapped.

## Names they already use

Use the name on the door and the name locals say. If those differ, pick the one a taxi driver knows, and mention the other once on the room's page. Do not invent a third name for the website.

If the rooms cook differently, they should be visible as text in the header or in one tap from Restaurants. Do not hide three venues behind a single photograph that advances on a timer. A guest looking for the quieter room should see its name.

Match the menu to the page headings. If the page says "Private dining" and the header says "Gatherings," you have split the offer. Pick the plainer word and use it in the header, the heading, and the button.

Hours and location are not a menu item called Info if you can put them on the restaurant page in the first screen. A separate Info page becomes a drawer. Drawers are where Tuesday's closure goes to be missed.

Test the labels on someone who has never eaten with you. Ask them to find tonight's menu for a named room and to book a table for two. If they hesitate, change the word. Do not ask them to enjoy the puzzle.

## One path to the menu or the table

Book a table is the action, and it should look like one. It can sit at the end of the list and on each room. The words must match. "Reserve," "Book," and "Join" are three temperatures. Choose one.

The dangerous version is a single Book that opens a widget with the wrong venue selected. Test the link from every room. The path is wrong if the guest has to re-pick the restaurant inside the widget after they already picked it on your site.

Menu is the other path, and it should open the menu for that room, as HTML a phone can scroll. A PDF is a last resort you have tested. A menu item that downloads a group PDF with all venues mixed is how someone orders from the wrong kitchen.

On a phone, Book and the restaurant names should be available without sitting through a logo animation. A bar with the room names and Book, plus a short menu for private dining, is enough. A hamburger that hides dinner punishes the guest you most want.

If the header and the rooms have drifted, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the current menu and the last week of "which restaurant is this?" messages. The work is usually a relabel and a set of links that remember the venue. Hanabi designs and builds the site so those labels stay text, not pictures of a menu. You should be able to rename a room without reshooting the header.

## Several rooms, one list

Sort the rooms the way a guest chooses. By neighborhood, if that is the decision. By the kind of night, if one is a wine bar and one is a long dinner. Do not sort by the date you opened them, if that hides the room that is actually open tonight.

Each item in the list needs the name, the area, and today's hours as text. A mosaic of untitled crops is a desktop souvenir. The guest should not have to guess which square is which door.

The homepage can feature one room. The navigation still promises the others. If Restaurants leads to a page with one film and no names, the menu has over-promised. Fix the page.

Search is optional. Three rooms do not need a search box. A clear list beats a search that cannot spell the name. Add search when the group is large enough that a list is a chore. Do not add it to look complete.

## The phone menu

Design the small screen as the real menu. Same order. Type a thumb can hit. The list should not be a translucent layer over a moving plate. Close it, and the room should still be there.

The open state should be dismissible and usable without a pointer. WCAG's operable principle is the reminder. People have to use the control, not only admire it.

Do not invent a smaller information architecture for the phone. If private dining matters, it stays. If a journal does not deserve a place on the phone, it does not deserve the header on the desktop either.

Check it outside, one-handed, at the time people book. If you cannot reach the right room's menu in a few seconds, a guest comparing three groups will not try harder. The building can have several volumes. The entrance still needs a name.

## Labels that send people to the wrong night

A few patterns fail in the same way. "Explore" as the path to restaurants. A single item called Group that contains rooms, jobs, press, and a manifesto. Icon-only navigation, where a fork is supposed to mean menus. A menu that changes per page so there is no stable way to the other room.

Dropdowns that vanish before a tap fail on the phone. Open on tap, and keep the list still. Hover menus are a desktop habit that eats bookings.

If the office loves a poetic word, let it live in a sentence on the about page. The navigation is infrastructure. Infrastructure should be dull and exact. Dull is how the right table gets booked.

### A pass with a real booking

Do the test on a phone that is not logged into your tools. Start from a search or from the homepage, not from the design file. Find a named room. Open its menu. Start a booking and stop before you pay or confirm, unless you are on a staging widget. Note every time the venue resets, the PDF fails, or the label you trusted is missing.

Write down the three breaks. Fix those before you add a new item to the header. Most navigation problems in a restaurant group are a wrong deep link, a PDF, and a poetic word standing where a room name should be. They are not a lack of menu animation.

Repeat the pass for private dining if you offer it. The path should not dump a buyout into the two-top widget. If it does, the header is promising a product the link cannot deliver. Change the link or change the label. Do not leave both in disagreement through a weekend service.

Ask one host to do the same pass after a shift. They know the questions guests actually ask. If the host cannot find Tuesday's hours from the header, the guest will not either. Put the hours on the room page the header lands on, in text, and stop calling that a design detail. It is the navigation finishing its job.

Do the pass once for each room, not only the flagship. A group site often gets the famous door right and the second door wrong. The second door is where a mislabeled link quietly empties a dining room. Open that menu. Start that booking. Read that neighborhood out loud. If the header item and the landing page disagree by even a suburb, fix the pair before service. Write the result in a shared note the manager can see. Navigation is not finished when the desktop review looks balanced. It is finished when every name in the list lands on the night that name promises, on a phone, with the menu and the table still attached.

## The pictures those labels open

A clear menu still delivers the guest to images. If Restaurants opens on a logo animation, the navigation did its job and the first frame undid it. The next decision is what the photographs argue: the room and one dish, not a mood under a monogram.

That is [photography direction for a restaurant group](/blog/photography-direction-for-a-restaurant-group). Set the labels so the pictures have a true place to land. Then make the landing a room someone could book, with the dish in the frame and the words in the page.
